title: Moses' excuses (Exodus 4:10–17)
hook: I'm slow of speech; send someone else, please
carry: I will be with your mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, a name that is a verb: I am that I am, four letters printed LORD. Your line was I am that I am.

Reasons not to are easy to find. I'm not qualified. I'm not ready. Someone else would be better at this. At the burning bush, Moses runs through the whole list. First: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? God says, I will be with you. Second: what's your name? God answers, I AM. Third: what if they don't believe me? God gives him signs, a staff that turns into a snake, a hand that turns white and back. A talking fire, a new name for God, miracles on demand. But Moses has two more excuses left.
screen: `WHO AM I?` → `WHAT IS YOUR NAME?` → `THEY WON'T BELIEVE ME.`

segments.voice: The fourth, in the King James Bible: "O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." In Hebrew, heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue. Nobody knows exactly what that means. Some readers think Moses had a stammer; some, that he'd lost his Egyptian after years in the desert. A later Jewish story tells of the baby Moses burning his tongue on a coal in Pharaoh's palace. The Bible itself just says heavy. God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" Then today's line: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say." Not, I'll fix your mouth. I'll be with it. Then the fifth excuse, stripped of reasons: "O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send." Send someone else. Please. Here, the text says, God's anger burns. And still God doesn't give up on him. Your brother Aaron can speak well, God says, and he's already on his way to meet you. He'll be your mouth, I'll be with both your mouths, and take the staff. So the reluctant one goes, with help. Paul writes that God chose the weak things of the world. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child; Isaiah, that his lips are unclean. The Bible's leaders keep beginning with I can't, and keep being told, I will be with you.
screen: `HEAVY OF MOUTH, HEAVY OF TONGUE.` · `WHO HATH MADE MAN'S MOUTH?` · `SEND SOMEONE ELSE.` · `AARON WILL SPEAK WITH YOU.` · then, large: `I WILL BE WITH THY MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Think of something you feel pulled toward but keep avoiding, and listen for the excuse you reach for: not qualified, not the right time, someone else would do it better. Don't argue with it; just name it plainly, the way Moses finally did, then ask who your Aaron might be. If you pray, you can bring both to God.
Moses' excuses. Five reasons Moses gave at the burning bush not to go, ending with the plainest one: please send someone else.
Your line: I will be with your mouth. Clumsy words can still carry a calling. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Christians return to Moses's excuses when they feel called to something and unready for it, and Exodus 4 is preached to people nervous about speaking, teaching or serving.

original.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth. Moses's phrase for his speech, which the KJV gives as slow of speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses was a born leader and a great speaker.
what it means: he gave five excuses, ending with send someone else, and went only with a promise and a brother.
what a scholar hears: kevad peh, heavy of mouth, may mean a speech difficulty or simply lack of eloquence; later Jewish tradition told a story about a coal to explain it.

chat.says: I'm asked to lead something, but I'm a terrible speaker. Did Moses ever feel like that?
options: Yes. He said he was slow of speech, and God said, I will be with your mouth, and sent Aaron.
No. Moses never doubted himself; he agreed the moment God asked him to go.
Yes, so God healed his tongue on the spot, and he never struggled again.
chat.meaning: Moses said he was heavy of mouth. God didn't fix his mouth but promised to be with it, and sent Aaron to help.

Aaron.meaning: Moses's brother, who could speak well

Jeremiah.meaning: a prophet who protested that he was only a child

Isaiah.meaning: a prophet who said his lips were unclean

eloquent.meaning: able to speak smoothly and well

notes: The coal story is from Exodus Rabbah 1:26 (a later midrash); presented as 'a later Jewish story'. Confirm citation.
The five objections (3:11, 3:13, 4:1, 4:10, 4:13) are a common way of counting; confirm.
Prophets protesting (Jeremiah 1:6 too young; Isaiah 6:5 unclean lips) and 1 Corinthians 1:27 paraphrased.
Aaron 'already on his way' paraphrases 4:14 ('he cometh forth to meet thee').
